**FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE**


**Impossible Metals’ Eureka II Recovers Itself From the Ocean, Fully Autonomously**


*New footage from Halifax shows the American ocean-technology company’s underwater vehicle find its surface vessel beneath the waves, align, attach, and return to the deck with no human hand on the controls, clearing one of the gating hurdles to scalable ocean robotics.*


**PITTSBURGH, PA — August 24, 2026 —** Impossible Metals, an American ocean-technology company, today released footage of a live offshore demonstration in which its Eureka II vehicle recovered itself from the open ocean without human intervention. Beneath the wave zone, the autonomous vehicle located its surface vessel, aligned to it, attached with an integrated smart hook, and returned to the deck on its own, clearing one of the hardest problems standing between subsea robotics and commercial scale.


The vehicle paired acoustic positioning to find the vessel with visual guidance to align to it, then completed the connection through a mechanical smart hook that secured the vehicle for retrieval from the water. The full recovery sequence ran autonomously, with no operator controlling the vehicle at any point.


“Autonomous recovery is a gating function. If a subsea platform cannot reliably retrieve itself in real ocean conditions, outside a lab, it cannot scale,” said Jason Gilham, chief technology officer of Impossible Metals. “Halifax shows it working in open water, and it shows it working the way it will have to work every day in the field.”


**From capability to scalable operations**


Autonomous docking and recovery underpin the economics of sustained deployment. Every recovery that runs without a crew intervening reduces vessel downtime and cost, enables higher-frequency deployment cycles, lowers human risk, and raises how much of the time the system is actually working. For investors, that is the shift that matters: from single-mission robotics to repeatable, systemized ocean operations, the threshold widely viewed as necessary for commercial viability in subsea environments.


**An American capability for responsible ocean access**


The milestone comes amid intensifying global focus on critical minerals, subsea infrastructure, and ocean data, areas where access and environmental accountability increasingly go together. As an American company, Impossible Metals is building Eureka II to enable responsible access to ocean resources while meeting rising expectations for precision and environmental stewardship.


“The next generation of ocean capability will be defined by autonomy and precision, doing more with a lighter touch and proving it at every step,” said Steve Curnutte, executive chairman of Impossible Metals. “That is the standard we are building to, and it is how responsible access to the ocean should be earned.”


**# # #**


**About Impossible Metals**


Impossible Metals is an American ocean-technology company developing robotics and AI for precise, selective, and environmentally responsible interaction with the ocean. Its Eureka platform integrates robotics, sensing, and autonomy to enable a new model of subsea operations.
